UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape	)
)                              Docket No. AD26-8-000


PRE-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OF BRIAN STARLING, DIRECTOR OF ELECTRIC TRANSMISSION SYSTEM OPERATIONS CENTER, DOMINION ENERGY, INC.

On behalf of Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion Energy” or “Company”), I am honored to participate in the upcoming Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) technical conference on October 21, 2026. The purpose of this statement is to summarize my key remarks for Panel 1: “The State of Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape – Operational Challenges of Integrating Large Load in Evolving System Dynamics.” 

Dominion Energy’s subsidiaries operate as load serving entities, electric transmission owners, and an electric transmission provider. The Company has a long history of interconnecting data centers and other large load customers. In fact, Dominion Energy serves the largest data center market in the world and estimates total energy usage across its service territory to double in less than 15 years.  Much of this load is located in Northern Virginia, which is commonly referred to as “Data Center Alley.” As a result, Dominion Energy offers a unique and important perspective on how large load customers can connect to the Bulk Electric System (“BES”) without compromising reliability.

The rapid growth of data centers, AI compute campuses, cryptocurrency facilities, and other large computational loads represents a fundamental shift in how electric utilities, planners, and reliability coordinators must approach system planning. Historically, load was treated largely as passive demand. Today's large computational loads exhibit operational characteristics more similar to generation resources or inverter-based resources (“IBRs”) than traditional retail load. These facilities can rapidly change demand, transfer to onsite generation, or respond to grid disturbances in ways that materially affect bulk power system reliability. Recent large-load disturbance events have highlighted several important lessons. The first is the necessity of validated dynamic load models. Traditional static load assumptions are insufficient for facilities capable of losing or restoring hundreds or thousands of megawatts within seconds. Second, commissioning and witness testing procedures must expand beyond normal load pickup and include disturbance ride-through, voltage recovery, frequency response, and transfer-to-backup-generation performance. Third, mandatory disturbance monitoring at the point of interconnection is necessary to validate actual behavior and improve future models. The point of interconnection for the majority of Dominion Energy’s data centers occurs on the distribution system meaning this additional observability is needed down at the circuit and meter. Finally, planners must recognize that reliability boundaries increasingly extend beyond the utility-owned facilities and into customer-owned systems whose controls and protection can materially impact bulk system performance.

Accurate load forecasting also serves as a critical input to these important planning decisions. Dominion Energy uses historical metered data to power its load forecasting with the added distinction of capturing requested capacity and anticipated demand as two separate contributing inputs. The Company also breaks down data centers into different classes based on characteristics such as load factors, ramp rates and daily operations – all of which impact total energy usage. Contracts or Engineering Letters of Authorization (“ELOAs”) are used as a final step to validate – not create – the load forecast. Following this playbook, Dominion Energy has consistently forecasted data center load with unrivaled precision. Over a period of seven years, looking at an average of 3.5 GW of new data center load per year, the Company’s 16-month and 28-month-out load forecasts have fallen within plus or minus 100 megawatts (“MW”) and 200 MW; this equates to load forecasting accuracy levels between 94 and 97 percent. 

One of the emerging concerns regarding large loads connecting to the grid is unplanned data center load transfers. Recent events on Dominion Energy’s system underscore the importance of this concern. On Wednesday, July 10, 2024, a 230 kilovolt (“kV”) line locked out after a lightning arrester failed. No direct customer load was impacted, but approximately 1,500 megawatts (“MW”) of data center load at multiple sites transferred to on-site back-up generation during protection reclosing. The system performed as designed, and the fault cleared in standard order. However, the sudden transfer of load caused a sharp increase in voltage which had to be manually restored by system operators. It is important to note the customer load transfer off of the grid – not the fault clearing – created the resulting grid concern. On Monday, February 17, 2025, a similar event occurred when a different 230 kV line locked out due to tree contact outside of the right of way. The system again performed as designed and cleared the fault, but sensitive data center equipment saw the disturbance. This time approximately 1,700 MW of data center load transferred to on-site back-up generation.  Finally on July 22, 2026, a sub conductor on a 230 kV line failed causing a phase-to-phase fault which locked out the line.  Like the previous two events, the system performed as designed. This time 3,900 MW of load transferred offline after the initial fault.  

Analysis of these events have provided significant insights to the behavior of the BES and the impact of large loads and highlight the need to standardize the dynamic response of data centers during system faults. By understanding the operation, load characteristics, and protection settings of data centers, utilities can better predict their specific responses to similar events. This knowledge is essential for informing future strategies aimed at enhancing system resilience and mitigating the impact of such faults. To this end, utilities and data centers need open and transparent communication between engineers and leadership – preferably taking place early in the interconnection process but also throughout the ongoing relationship. Collaboration will be critical to preventing future load transfers and subsequent voltage and frequency excursions on the BES.
Reliability challenges are increasingly being observed across North America as IBRs such as solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and other power-electronic technologies replace conventional synchronous generation. As rotating mass declines, system operators are seeing greater sensitivity to frequency excursions, voltage instability, and oscillatory events following disturbances. The industry’s focus should be on defining the reliability services needed to maintain a secure and resilient grid to ensure new resources are capable of providing them. Advanced technologies such as next-generation BESS, grid-forming inverters, flexible AC transmission systems, synchronous condensers, and emerging resources including small modular reactors can all play a role in supplying essential reliability services. Reliability frameworks should establish performance-based requirements that allow resource owners to meet reliability objectives through proven, cost-effective solutions. At the same time, planning engineers and operators should continue strengthening planning and operational practices through improved modeling, ride-through requirements, dynamic performance assessments, and interconnection standards that recognize the changing characteristics of the resource mix and increasing penetration of large loads.
The electric industry is already taking meaningful steps to address the impacts of declining system inertia and evolving grid dynamics. Utilities, regional transmission organizations (“RTOs”), and reliability organizations are enhancing modeling standards, validating IBR performance, and requiring both generation resources and large loads to remain connected and support the grid during disturbances. As large loads continue to interconnect, particularly in areas experiencing rapid economic growth, planners must evaluate not only thermal loading concerns but also dynamic factors such as frequency response, voltage recovery, system strength, and control-system interactions. In parallel, cybersecurity and physical security remain critical considerations. Large loads often depend on extensive communications, automation, and operational technology systems that create unique security challenges depending on the customer type. Data centers, industrial facilities, and other large customers each present different operational characteristics, but all require a comprehensive security approach. Dominion Energy has long employed a layered strategy that integrates cybersecurity protections, physical security measures, continuous monitoring, and close coordination with customers and industry partners to ensure that reliability and security considerations are addressed throughout the interconnection and operational lifecycle.
From an integrated utility perspective, maintaining reliability amid significant load growth also requires close coordination between electric and natural gas infrastructure. Whether evaluating behind-the-meter gas-fired generation or front-of-meter generating resources, utilities must understand the dependencies that exist between gas supply, transportation capacity, and electric system operations. Effective coordination between gas and electric sectors enables more informed planning and strengthens system resilience during periods of high demand or system stress. This is most important during the extreme colds experienced across the country.  As data centers and other large-load customers create increasingly flat and sustained load shapes, utilities and RTOs are placing greater emphasis on fuel security, generation diversity, firm fuel arrangements, and long-term infrastructure planning to ensure sufficient capacity is available when customers need it most.
Thank you again for the opportunity to provide comments. I look forward to the discussion.

Sincerely,



J. Brian Starling
